title: Numerical Linear Algebra
markdown: ## What this covers Nearly every statistical and machine-learning method — linear regression, its more elaborate relatives, deep networks, PCA and its many variants — bottoms out in matrix multiplication and some matrix decomposition. This chapter is the numerical-linear-algebra toolkit behind that: how to read the standard notation, what rank, invertibility and definiteness mean in statistical terms (not just algebraic ones), why a computation that is mathematically equivalent to another can be wildly different in cost or in accuracy, and the handful of matrix factorizations — LU, Cholesky, QR, eigendecomposition, SVD — that a computer actually uses to solve $Ax = b$, fit a regression, or run a PCA. It assumes ordinary matrix algebra (multiplication, transpose, inverse) and the earlier material on how computers represent numbers: floating-point precision and catastrophic cancellation are taken as background and referred to rather than re-derived. ## Notation and a working vocabulary Capital letters denote matrices, $A$, lower-case letters denote vectors, $x$. Then $x_i$ is the $i$th element of $x$, $A_{ij}$ is the $(i,j)$ entry, $A_{\cdot j}$ is the $j$th column and $A_{i \cdot}$ the $i$th row. A vector $x$ is by default a one-column matrix, so $x^\top$ is a one-row matrix. Matrices in an operation have to be **conformable**: $A + B$ needs matching dimensions, and $AB$ needs the number of columns of $A$ to match the number of rows of $B$ (a column vector is just a one-column matrix, so this covers $Ab$ too). Checking dimensions is a cheap way to catch errors — for example, if $A$ is $m \times n$, is $\mathrm{Cov}(Ax) = A\,\mathrm{Cov}(x)\,A^\top$ or $A^\top \mathrm{Cov}(x)\, A$? Only the first is conformable. The **inner product** of two vectors is $\sum_i x_i y_i = x^\top y \equiv \langle x, y \rangle$; the **outer product** is $xy^\top$, built from all pairwise products of the entries. ### Norms and orthogonality For a vector, $\|x\|_p = (\sum_i |x_i|^p)^{1/p}$; the Euclidean norm $\|x\|_2 = \sqrt{x^\top x}$ is just the length of $x$, written $\|x\|$ unless noted otherwise. For a matrix, the **Frobenius norm** is $\|A\|_F = (\sum_{i,j} A_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$, but the more important one for this chapter is the **induced norm**, defined relative to a vector norm as $$\|A\| = \sup_{x \neq 0} \frac{\|Ax\|}{\|x\|}, \qquad \|A\|_2 = \sup_{\|x\|_2 = 1} \|Ax\|_2 .$$ Read the supremum as "maximum" if that is unfamiliar. The induced norm is **the most a matrix can stretch a vector**, relative to the vector's own length, and — this will matter later — the 2-norm of $A$ turns out to equal the largest singular value in the SVD of $A$. Any legitimate matrix norm satisfies $\|AB\| \leq \|A\|\|B\|$ and the triangle inequality $\|A+B\| \leq \|A\| + \|B\|$. A vector is normalized when $\|x\| = 1$; any vector is normalized by $\tilde{x} = x/\|x\|$, and the angle between two vectors is $\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\big(\langle x,y\rangle / \sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle \langle y,y\rangle}\big)$. Two vectors are **orthogonal** if $x^\top y = 0$. A square matrix is **orthogonal** if its columns (equivalently its rows) are orthogonal to each other and normalized. Orthogonal matrices have full rank, satisfy $A^\top A = I$ (so $A^{-1} = A^\top$), and have determinant $\pm 1$. The product of two orthogonal matrices is orthogonal, since $(AB)^\top AB = B^\top A^\top A B = B^\top B = I$. A **permutation matrix** — one that swaps two rows or columns of another matrix under multiplication — is a special orthogonal matrix: an *elementary* permutation matrix has determinant $-1$, and products of these give the more general permutation matrices, still orthogonal. Premultiplying by $P$ permutes rows; postmultiplying permutes columns. On a computer this is essentially free: rather than actually moving the entries of $A$ in memory, you can usually just rework the index bookkeeping that says where each row or column lives. ### Some standard identities $AB \neq BA$ in general, but $A + B = B + A$ and $A(BC) = (AB)C$. The **trace** (sum of diagonal entries) is linear, $\mathrm{tr}(A+B) = \mathrm{tr}(A) + \mathrm{tr}(B)$, $\mathrm{tr}(A) = \mathrm{tr}(A^\top)$, and — usefully — invariant under cyclic permutation of a product: $\mathrm{tr}(ABC) = \mathrm{tr}(CAB) = \mathrm{tr}(BCA)$. Two consequences: you can reorder a chain of non-square matrices to minimize computation, and a quadratic form can be rewritten as a trace, $x^\top A x = \mathrm{tr}(x^\top A x) = \mathrm{tr}(xx^\top A)$, which is often the move that lets a statistical calculation go back and forth between a scalar and a matrix expression. For square matrices, $|AB| = |A||B|$, hence $|A^{-1}| = 1/|A|$ (since $|I| = |AA^{-1}| = 1$), and $|A| = |A^\top|$ (seen via the QR decomposition, using that the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal and the determinant of an orthogonal matrix is $\pm 1$). For square invertible matrices, $(A^{-1})^\top = (A^\top)^{-1}$ — from $(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$ applied to $A^\top (A^{-1})^\top = (A^{-1}A)^\top = I$ — and $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$. Two other products come up: the **Hadamard (direct) product**, entrywise multiplication (`A * B` in R or Python), and the **Kronecker product**, $$A \otimes B = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11}B & \cdots & A_{1m}B \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ A_{n1}B & \cdots & A_{nm}B \end{pmatrix},$$ whose inverse is the Kronecker product of the inverses, $B^{-1} \otimes A^{-1}$ — a solve that costs $O(n^3 + m^3)$ instead of the $O((nm)^3)$ a naive inverse of the full Kronecker product would cost. Finally, a **matrix decomposition** re-expresses $A$ as a product of two or three simpler matrices that reveal structure in $A$ — simpler by having fewer rows or columns, by being diagonal, triangular or sparse, or by being orthogonal. Once you have a decomposition, computation with $A$ is generally much easier, because of the structure of the pieces. This is the subject of a later section. ## The key principle: form is not just mathematics, it is cost **The form of a mathematical expression and how it should be evaluated on a computer can be very different, and better computational approaches can both increase speed and improve the numerical properties of a calculation.** Three examples make the point: - If $X, Y$ are matrices and $z$ a vector, compute $X(Yz)$, not $(XY)z$: the former is far cheaper, since it only ever multiplies a matrix by a vector. - $(X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top Y$ is never computed by forming $X^\top X$ and inverting it — in some implementations $X^\top X$ is never formed at all (this is the reasoning behind fitting regression via the QR decomposition, below). - To permute two rows of a matrix $A$ with a permutation matrix $P$, a computer need not actually touch the values of $A$ in memory (for instance to compute $PAB$) — as noted above, it can just rework which index points at which row. ### Counting the cost: computational complexity Complexity is assessed by counting multiplies/divides and adds/subtracts (multiplication is slightly more expensive than addition, so some algorithms trade one for the other). Usually only the **order** of the count matters, written $O(f(n))$: the number of operations approaches $c f(n)$ as $n \to \infty$. Take matrix multiplication $AB$ with $A$ of size $a \times b$ and $B$ of size $b \times c$. Every entry of the product is an inner product of length $b$, and there are $ac$ such entries, so the total is $abc$ multiplies, $O(abc)$. For two symmetric $n\times n$ matrices this is $O(n^3)$, and matrix factorizations such as the Cholesky decomposition are also generically $O(n^3)$ unless the matrix has special structure (e.g. sparsity). Both time and memory scale badly with $n$: holding the inputs and output of the multiply above needs $ab+bc+ac$ elements, $3n^2$ for symmetric matrices, so for $n = 10{,}000$, $3\cdot(10{,}000)^2 \cdot 8 / 10^9 = 2.4$ Gb. $O(n^q)$ is *polynomial time*; $O(b^n)$ (*exponential time*) is much worse, $O(\log n)$ (*log time*) much better. (Problems with no polynomial-time algorithm are the NP-complete problems of computer science — all such problems can be rewritten as instances of one another.) The order does not tell the whole story in practice: an $O(n^2)$ algorithm can be slower than an $O(n\log n)$ one for realistic $n$, if the constant is large — $n^2$ operations versus $1000(n \log n + n)$, say, where $1000n$ alone can dominate for a long time. *Flops* — floating point operations, or floating point operations per second — is the standard unit for both operation counts and speed. ## What rank and invertibility mean statistically A set of vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is **linearly independent (LIN)** if none can be written as a linear combination of the others. At most $n$ length-$n$ vectors can be LIN. The **rank** of a matrix is the number of LIN rows, equivalently columns (always at most $\min(\text{rows}, \text{columns})$); it is most natural to think of it as the dimension of the column space. A set of LIN vectors spans a space consisting of all their linear combinations, and the spanning vectors are called **basis vectors**. Any $y$ in that space is $y = \sum_i c_i v_i$; if the basis is orthonormal, the weights are simply $c_i = \langle y, v_i \rangle$. **Regression is the natural place to see this.** With $p$ covariates (columns of the design matrix $X$), of which $q \leq p$ are LIN, $p - q$ columns are linear combinations of the other $q$, the column space has dimension $q$ rather than $p$, and $X^\top X$ has $p - q$ zero eigenvalues. The $q$ LIN columns are basis vectors for that space, playing the role of (non-orthogonal) axes: a point in the space is specified by $q$ coordinates exactly as a point in $\mathbb{R}^q$ is specified by coordinates along orthogonal axes. - If $n = p = q$, the $n$ observations sit *exactly* on the space spanned by the $p$ basis vectors (e.g. $n=p=2$ puts every point exactly on the simple-linear-regression line): a single exact solution, no residual. - If $n < p$, the rank is at most $n < p$, so the system is **underdetermined**: many solutions fit exactly, and choosing among them is the business of generalized inverses, below. - If $n > p$, the system is **overdetermined**: no exact solution exists, and regression is about minimizing some criterion (least squares, penalized least squares) on the gap between the observations and the space spanned by the columns of $X$. Geometrically this is exactly **projecting the observation vector onto the column space of $X$** — finding the closest point in that space to the observed $y$. ### Invertibility, singularity, rank, and definiteness, tied together For square matrices, invertibility, rank and definiteness are one story. A "regular" square matrix (symmetric matrices and matrices with distinct eigenvalues are regular, among others) has an eigendecomposition $A = \Gamma \Lambda \Gamma^{-1}$, with eigenvectors as the columns of $\Gamma$ and eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\Lambda$. The rank equals the number of non-zero eigenvalues; a square matrix is invertible (nonsingular) exactly when it has full rank; for symmetric $A$, $\Gamma$ is orthogonal, giving $A = \Gamma \Lambda \Gamma^\top$ and, when no eigenvalue is zero, $A^{-1} = \Gamma \Lambda^{-1} \Gamma^\top$. The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues, zero exactly when the rank is deficient. Among symmetric matrices, the ones that arise in statistics are **positive definite (p.d.)** or **non-negative definite (n.n.d.)**. $A$ is p.d. when $x^\top A x > 0$ for every $x \neq 0$. If $\mathrm{Cov}(y) = A$, then $x^\top A x = \mathrm{Var}(x^\top y)$, so positive definiteness says exactly that every linear combination of the underlying random variables has positive variance — **positive definite matrices are exactly (unconstrained) covariance matrices.** This chain of equivalences is worth having as one block: $$A \text{ p.d.} \iff A \text{ a covariance matrix} \iff x^\top A x > 0 \; \forall x \iff \lambda_i > 0 \; \forall i \implies |A| > 0 \implies A \text{ invertible} \iff A \text{ nonsingular} \iff A \text{ full rank},$$ and, for positive semi-definite (constrained covariance) matrices, $$A \text{ p.s.d.} \iff x^\top A x \geq 0 \text{ (}=0\text{ for some } x) \iff \lambda_i \geq 0 \text{, at least one zero} \implies |A| = 0 \iff A \text{ not invertible} \iff A \text{ singular} \iff A \text{ not full rank}.$$ Any crossproduct $X^\top X$ is p.d. (n.n.d. if $p > n$) — it is, after all, just a scaled empirical covariance matrix. **Interpreting the eigendecomposition generatively.** To generate $y$ with $\mathrm{Cov}(y) = A$, take $y = \Gamma \Lambda^{1/2} z$ with $\mathrm{Cov}(z) = I$: $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ is the standard deviation attached to the basis vector $\Gamma_{\cdot i}$, and $y$ is a linear combination of eigenvectors weighted by $z$ and scaled by the eigenvalues. Running this backwards, projecting $y$ onto the eigenvector basis gives $w = \Gamma^\top y = \Lambda^{1/2}z$ (using that $\Gamma$ is orthogonal). If $A$ is only p.s.d., one or more eigenvalues are zero, which raises three natural questions worth sitting with: what does a zero eigenvalue mean for $y$? what happens if you *round* a very small eigenvalue to zero? and, considering the **precision matrix** $A^{-1} = \Gamma \Lambda^{-1} \Gamma^\top$, what does a very large or very small diagonal entry of $\Lambda^{-1}$ correspond to? ### Generalized inverses (optional) To solve $Ax = b$, the mathematical answer is $x = A^{-1}b$ when $A$ is invertible. When $A$ is not full rank, a **generalized inverse** $A^-$ (satisfying $AA^-A = A$) plays that role instead. The **Moore–Penrose inverse** (pseudo-inverse) $A^+$ is the unique generalized inverse with additional properties, and $x = A^+ b$ is the *minimum-length* solution of $Ax=b$ among all solutions. The pseudo-inverse is built from the eigendecomposition (or the SVD, below) as $\Gamma \Lambda^+ \Gamma^\top$, where $\Lambda^+$ inverts every positive $\lambda_i$ and leaves the zero ones at zero. Statistically: a zero eigenvalue of a precision matrix means infinite variance along that basis vector; the pseudo-inverse instead assigns that direction *zero* variance. **Worked example.** Autoregressive (AR) models are used for smoothing in time, space, or covariates. A first-order AR model, $E(y_i \mid y_{-i}) = \tfrac12(y_{i-1}+y_{i+1})$, has precision matrix (band structure, edges omitted) $$\begin{pmatrix} \ddots & & \vdots \\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ \cdots & -1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots \\ & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ & & \vdots & & \ddots \end{pmatrix},$$ and a second-order model, $E(y_i\mid y_{-i}) = \tfrac16(4y_{i-1}+4y_{i+1}-y_{i-2}-y_{i+2})$, has a similarly banded but wider precision matrix. In the first-order case the eigenvector associated with the *constant* vector has eigenvalue exactly zero — checkable directly: ```python import numpy as np precMat = np.array([[1,-1,0,0,0],[-1,2,-1,0,0],[0,-1,2,-1,0], [0,0,-1,2,-1],[0,0,0,-1,1]]) e = np.linalg.eig(precMat) e[0] # 4th eigenvalue is numerically zero e[1][:, 3] # the constant eigenvector ``` There is no information about the overall level of $y$, so we cannot put infinite variance on that direction and still generate samples — instead we take the pseudo-inverse, giving it zero variance, which amounts to generating under the constraint $\sum y_i = \bar y = 0$: ```python evals = e[0] evals = 1 / evals # variances evals[3] = 0 # generalized inverse: zero variance on the constant direction rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1) y = e[1] @ ((evals ** 0.5) * rng.normal(size=5)) ``` The second-order model has *two* non-identifiabilities (level and linear trend). One way to use this in a model is to write $\mu + y$, with $y$ given the generalized-inverse covariance above: this allows a genuine mean $\mu$ (and, in the second-order case, a linear term) on top of the smooth autoregressive variation that the singular precision matrix alone cannot supply. ### The matrices that arise in regression $X^\top X$ is symmetric and non-negative definite, which is exactly why $(X^\top X)^{-1}$ appears in the OLS estimator — but it fails to be positive definite (and hence not invertible) precisely when $X$'s columns are not all linearly independent. The fitted values are $X\hat\beta = X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top Y = HY$: the **hat matrix** $H$ projects $Y$ onto the column space of $X$, and is **idempotent**, $HH = H$ — reprojecting something already in the space changes nothing. $H$ itself is singular (its rank equals the rank of $X$, which is ordinarily less than the $n$ dimensions it lives in) — worth asking under exactly what circumstance that would fail to hold, and $H$ would be the identity instead. ## Storage layout and algorithm order Retrieving matrix entries from memory is fastest when they are contiguous, so a **column-major** language (R, Fortran) favors working a column (or all columns) at a time, while a **row-major** language (Python, C) favors working a row at a time. Some implementations of matrix factorizations save space (and time) by overwriting the input's memory with the output. Beyond storage, the *order* of an algorithm — not just its asymptotic cost — matters. Computing $b = Ax$ can be organized as inner products of the rows of $A$ with $x$ (accessing $A$ by row: good for row-major storage) or as a linear combination of the columns of $A$ weighted by $x$ (accessing $A$ by column: good for column-major storage); both involve the same number of operations, but which is faster in practice depends on the memory layout and on how big the matrices are. The same caveats as ordinary computer arithmetic apply throughout linear algebra, simply because it involves arithmetic on many elements: good implementations stay alert to catastrophic cancellation and to dividing by values at or near zero. ## Ill-conditioning A problem is **ill-conditioned** if small changes to the inputs produce large changes to the output — quantified by a **condition number**, which depends on the operation. The condition number that matters most here is with respect to *matrix inversion*: under the $L_2$ norm, it is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue (in absolute value). **Worked example.** Take $$A = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 7 & 8 & 7 \\ 7 & 5 & 6 & 5 \\ 8 & 6 & 10 & 9 \\ 7 & 5 & 9 & 10 \end{pmatrix}.$$ Solving $Ax=b$ for $b = (32,23,33,31)$ gives $x = (1,1,1,1)$, but the tiny perturbation $b + \delta b = (32.1, 22.9, 33.1, 30.9)$ gives $x + \delta x = (9.2, -12.6, 4.5, -1.1)$ — a huge swing from a small nudge. ```python def norm2(x): return (np.sum(x**2)) ** 0.5 A = np.array([[10,7,8,7],[7,5,6,5],[8,6,10,9],[7,5,9,10]]) b, bPerturbed = np.array([32,23,33,31]), np.array([32.1,22.9,33.1,30.9]) x, xPerturbed = np.linalg.solve(A, b), np.linalg.solve(A, bPerturbed) ``` Manipulating the induced-norm inequalities (any induced norm; take it to be the Euclidean one) gives $$\frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|} \leq \|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|\,\frac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}, \qquad \mathrm{cond}(A) \equiv \|A\|\|A^{-1}\|,$$ and for a nonsingular square matrix under the $L_2$ norm this condition number is exactly the ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue magnitude — since $\|A\|_2$ is the largest eigenvalue magnitude of $A$, and $\|A^{-1}\|_2$, being the largest eigenvalue magnitude of $A^{-1}$, is the *reciprocal* of the smallest eigenvalue magnitude of $A$. The wide spread of eigenvalues in $A$ above is exactly why the relative perturbation in $x$ is so much larger than the relative perturbation in $b$, with the condition number giving an upper bound on the ratio. More concretely, on a computer the system actually solved is $(A + \delta A)(x + \delta x) = b + \delta b$, where the perturbation comes from finite floating-point precision: $\|\delta b\|/\|b\| \approx \|\delta A\|/\|A\| \approx 10^{-p}$, with $p = 16$ for standard double precision. This gives (following Gentle, and valid only when $10^{t-p} \ll 1$) $$\frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|} \approx \mathrm{cond}(A)\cdot 10^{-p},$$ so if $\mathrm{cond}(A) \approx 10^t$, the accuracy achieved is order $10^{t-p}$ rather than $10^{-p}$: **the condition number, on a log scale, is the number of digits of accuracy lost** relative to the machine's native precision. A condition number of $10^8$ loses 8 of the 16 digits double precision normally carries. (Estimating the condition number is itself subject to numerical error, and — except for the $L_2$ norm on a square nonsingular matrix — requires $A^{-1}$; see Golub and Van Loan for an algorithm that avoids this.) ### Improving conditioning In statistics, ill-conditioning most often comes from **collinearity** among regressors, and the best fix is usually not numerical but statistical — rethinking the model, since ill-conditioning here is a symptom of a substantive problem, not just an implementation detail. Numerically, the general advice is to avoid large disparities in the magnitudes of the numbers involved, which **centering and scaling** achieves in a regression context. **Worked example.** Regress on calendar years $t = 1990, \ldots, 2010$ with a quadratic term: ```python t1 = np.arange(1990, 2011) X1 = np.column_stack((np.ones(len(t1)), t1, t1**2)) beta = np.array([5, 0.1, 0.0001]) y = X1 @ beta + rng.normal(size=len(t1)) np.linalg.cond(X1.T @ X1) # very large sm.OLS(y, X1).fit().params # intercept & linear term way off ``` The naive covariate produces wildly spread eigenvalues in $X_1^\top X_1$, and the fitted intercept and linear coefficient come out far from the truth — not because OLS is a poor estimator of $\beta$, but because of the ill-conditioning itself. Centering the covariate, ```python t2 = t1 - 2000 X2 = np.column_stack((np.ones(len(t1)), t2, t2**2)) ``` fixes the intercept and linear term (the *true* values on the centered scale are $(605, 0.5, 0.0001)$, from expanding $\beta_0 + \beta_1((t-c)+c) + \beta_2((t-c)+c)^2$ at $c=2000$) — interestingly, the quadratic coefficient was *already* accurate before centering, for reasons that are not entirely obvious from this alone. Scaling further, $t_3 = t_2/10$, improves the conditioning again. The rule of thumb: work with numbers of magnitude around 1 — change units (income in thousands rather than dollars) rather than fight the raw scale. ## Solving linear systems: factorizations Numerically, $Ax = b$ is essentially never solved by forming $A^{-1}$ and multiplying; instead a matrix decomposition (or an equivalent set of steps) is used — Gaussian elimination, equivalent to an LU decomposition, or a Cholesky decomposition when $A$ is positive (semi-)definite. Iterative methods (see the closing section) trade an exact answer for less computation, provided they are stopped early. The standard decompositions, adapted from Gentle (*Computational Statistics*, Table 5.1): | Name | Representation | Restrictions | Properties | Uses | |---|---|---|---|---| | LU | $A_{nn} = L_{nn}U_{nn}$ | $A$ generally square | $L$ lower, $U$ upper triangular | solving equations; inversion | | QR | $A_{nm}=Q_{nn}R_{nm}$ or (skinny) $A_{nm}=Q_{nm}R_{mm}$ | | $Q$ orthogonal; $R$ upper triangular | regression | | Cholesky | $A_{nn} = U_{nn}^\top U_{nn}$ | $A$ positive (semi-)definite | $U$ upper triangular | multivariate normal; covariance; solving equations; inversion | | Eigendecomposition | $A_{nn} = \Gamma_{nn}\Lambda_{nn}\Gamma_{nn}^\top$ | $A$ square, symmetric | $\Gamma$ orthogonal; $\Lambda$ diagonal | PCA and related | | SVD | $A_{nm}=U_{nn}D_{nm}V_{mm}^\top$ (or thin) | | $U,V$ orthogonal; $D$ diagonal, non-negative | machine learning, topic models | The notes here spend most of their time on the QR, deferring the mechanics of Gaussian elimination/LU and of Cholesky to recorded derivations (see Sources) rather than the written text; what follows covers the piece that *is* written out in full: reducing any of these factorizations to a **triangular solve**, and then the QR family in detail. ### Triangular systems: the common last step Every factorization above ends the same way — with a triangular system to solve. If $A$ is upper triangular, $Ax = b$ is solved from the bottom up (a **backsolve**): $x_n = b_n / A_{nn}$ trivially, then for each $k < n$ in decreasing order, plug in the already-known $x_{k+1}, \ldots, x_n$ and solve the $k$th equation for $x_k$. (Lower triangular systems solve the same way from the top, sometimes called a forward-solve.) This is the step every factorization in the table above reduces to, and it is cheap: linear systems become fast exactly because triangular ones are. ### The QR decomposition Any $X_{n\times p}$ (with $n \geq p$) factors as $X = QR$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $R$ upper triangular. If $n > p$, only the leading $p$ rows of $R$ are non-zero, giving the **skinny QR**, $X = Q_1 R_1$ (what R's `qr()` returns), and only the first $p$ columns of $Q$ are needed. Fixing the sign convention so $R$'s diagonal is non-negative makes $R$ exactly the upper-triangular Cholesky factor of $X^\top X$: $X^\top X = R^\top Q^\top Q R = R^\top R$. There are three standard ways to compute the QR — **reflections** (Householder), **rotations** (Givens), or **Gram–Schmidt** orthogonalization — covered below. For $n\times n$ $X$, the Householder approach costs $2n^3/3$ flops, making QR less efficient than LU or Cholesky. The pseudo-inverse of $X$ falls out of the QR too: $X^+ = [R_1^{-1}\ 0]\,Q^\top$ (with a pivoted variant handling the case where $X$ is not full rank). **Why fit regression with the QR.** Writing $Y = X\beta + \epsilon$ and using the skinny QR (with $R^\top$ invertible), the normal equations $X^\top X \beta = X^\top Y$ become $$R^\top Q^\top Q R \beta = R^\top Q^\top Y \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R\beta = Q^\top Y,$$ which is just a backsolve. The standard regression quantities (hat matrix, SSE, residuals) all have clean expressions in $Q$ and $R$. The reason to prefer QR over Cholesky-on-$X^\top X$ is conditioning: the condition number of $X$ is the *square root* of that of $X^\top X$, so QR works with the better-conditioned object directly — though Monahan notes that the cases where this matters numerically tend to be cases (e.g. highly collinear predictors) where OLS itself is not particularly useful anyway. On raw operation counts, Cholesky is $np^2 + \tfrac13 p^3$, an algorithm called *sweeping* is $np^2+p^3$, Householder QR is $2np^2-\tfrac23p^3$, and modified Gram–Schmidt is $2np^2$ — so Cholesky (and sweeping) win when $n \gg p$, modified Gram–Schmidt is reportedly the most numerically stable of the four and sweeping the least, and since all of them are linear in $n$, the differences rarely matter much in practice. In Python, `Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)`; `statsmodels`' OLS fitter uses the QR internally. In R, `X.qr = qr(X); Q = qr.Q(X.qr); R = qr.R(X.qr)`, with companion functions `qr.resid()`, `qr.fitted()`, `qr.coef()` that express the usual regression quantities via $Q$ and $R$ directly. Both languages return the skinny QR by default: the first $p$ columns of $Q$ span the column space of $X$, and the remaining $n-p$ columns span its orthogonal complement — the "extra" dimensions of the observation space that regression does not use. #### Computing the QR: reflections and Gram–Schmidt **Householder reflections.** If $u,v$ are orthonormal and $x = c_1 u + c_2 v$, then $\tilde x = -c_1 u + c_2 v$ reflects $x$ across the hyperplane perpendicular to $u$ — a **Householder reflection**. The matrix $Q = I - 2uu^\top$ performs it: $Qu=-u$, $Qv=v$ whenever $u^\top v = 0$, and $Q$ is both orthogonal and symmetric. Building the QR is then a sequence of these: choose $u$ so that $Q_1 x = \tilde x = (\|x\|, 0,\ldots,0)$, which is achieved by $u = (x - \tilde x)/\|x-\tilde x\|$ applied to the first column of $X$, zeroing everything below the first entry; $Q_2$ then zeros the remaining entries of the second column, and so on, giving $R = Q_p \cdots Q_1 X$ and $Q = (Q_p\cdots Q_1)^\top$. (For numerical stability, the sign of $\tilde x_1$ is chosen opposite to $x_1$ at each step, to avoid cancelling two nearly-equal numbers in $x - \tilde x$.) Applied to a regression, the same transformations act on $Y$ to give $Q^\top Y$, which splits into a length-$p$ piece $z^{(1)}$ and a length-$(n-p)$ piece $z^{(2)}$, with $\mathrm{SSR} = \|z^{(1)}\|^2$ and $\mathrm{SSE} = \|z^{(2)}\|^2$. **Modified Gram–Schmidt** builds $Q$'s columns one at a time in the opposite spirit: normalize the first column of $X$ to get the first column of $Q$, then immediately remove that direction from *all* remaining columns; normalize the next column to get the next column of $Q$, remove that direction from what is left; and so on. (This "orthogonalize against the newest vector, applied to everything still remaining" order is the *modified* Gram–Schmidt, and is more numerically stable than the textbook version that orthogonalizes each vector against all previous ones at once, especially when the columns of $X$ are close to collinear.) Equivalently $R = Q^\top X$ — regressing the columns of $X$ on $Q$ — which is also why $R$ comes out upper triangular: the first column of $X$ is a multiple of the first column of $Q$, the second a combination of the first two columns of $Q$, and so on. ### The "tall-skinny" QR When $n \gg p$, the QR of $X$ can be computed in parallel by a nested divide-and-conquer: split $X$ into row blocks $X_0, X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots$, QR-factor each block separately to get $Q_iR_i$, then repeatedly stack pairs of $R$-factors and QR them again ($\binom{R_0}{R_1} = Q_{01}R_{01}$, etc.) until a single $R$ remains; $Q$ is then a product of block-diagonal orthogonal matrices built from the $Q_i$'s at each stage. This map-reduce-friendly scheme never needs to hold all of $X$ in memory at once — a serial variant processes one row-block at a time, stacking the running $R$ on top of the next block and re-factoring. ### Determinants, computed safely The absolute value of $|A|$ can be read off any factorization into a triangular (or diagonal) matrix times orthogonal matrices, since $|Q| = \pm 1$: $|A| = |QR| = \pm|R|$, and (for square $A$) $|A^\top A| = |R_1|^2$. Equivalently, use the product of the singular values in the SVD, or — for non-negative definite $A$, where the sign is never in doubt — the product of the diagonal of the Cholesky factor; or the product of the eigenvalues, $|A| = |\Lambda|$. Computing any of these products directly overflows or underflows for even moderate matrices, so determinants are **always** computed on the log scale, as a sum of logs (tracking the count of negative diagonal entries separately if signs are needed). Since a factorization is often already available from earlier in a computation, the determinant frequently comes for free. ## Eigendecomposition and the SVD ### Eigendecomposition The eigendecomposition (spectral decomposition) decomposes the components of variation into orthogonal patterns (eigenvectors) with associated variances (eigenvalues) — the natural language for PCA, and useful more generally for reasoning about the convergence of iterative algorithms. Square symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues/eigenvectors and $A = \Gamma\Lambda\Gamma^\top$ with eigenvalues ordered in decreasing value; $A^{-1} = \Gamma\Lambda^{-1}\Gamma^\top$ and a "square root" $\Gamma \Lambda^{1/2}$ follow immediately. The **spectral radius** $\rho(A)$, the largest eigenvalue magnitude, equals the induced 2-norm for symmetric matrices ($\rho(A)=\|A\|_2$), and satisfies $\rho(A) \leq \|A\|$ for any induced norm generally — it governs the convergence rate of some iterative algorithms (see below). **Computing it.** The standard method for the full eigendecomposition is the *QR algorithm*: reduce $A$ to upper Hessenberg form (upper triangular except possibly for one non-zero subdiagonal — actually tridiagonal, for symmetric $A$) via Householder or Givens transformations, then apply the QR decomposition repeatedly (with diagonal shifts) until the result converges to a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues; the eigenvectors come out as the accumulated product of the Householder matrices and the successive $Q$'s. If only the largest eigenvalue (or the largest few) is needed — common in time series and Markov chain problems — the simpler **power method** suffices: repeatedly multiply by $A$ and normalize, $v^{(k)} = Az^{(k-1)}$, $z^{(k)} = v^{(k)}/\|v^{(k)}\|$; a Markov chain reaching steady state via $x_t = A^t x_0$ is exactly this iteration. Deflating by the found eigenvector/eigenvalue pair and repeating extends this to the next few largest. ### Singular value decomposition For an $n\times m$ matrix $A$ (take $n \geq m$; otherwise work with $A^\top$) — representing, say, $m$ features of $n$ observations, or $n$ documents by $m$ words, or $n$ genes by $m$ conditions — the **SVD** is $A = UDV^\top$, with $U,V$ orthonormal-column matrices and $D$ diagonal and non-negative. Restricting to rank $k=\mathrm{rank}(A)$, $$A_{n\times m} = U_{n\times k}D_{k\times k}V_{k\times m}^\top = \sum_{j=1}^k D_{jj}\,u_j v_j^\top,$$ a sum of rank-one matrices, each a scaled outer product. If $A$ is p.s.d., its eigendecomposition *is* an SVD; in general $A^\top A = VD^2V^\top$ and $AA^\top = UD^2U^\top$, so the singular values squared are the eigenvalues of both crossproducts. **What it is used for.** The SVD gives the rank of $A$ and its pseudo-inverse, $A^+ = VD^+U^\top$. Truncating to the largest $p < k$ terms, $A \approx \tilde A = \sum_{j=1}^p D_{jj}u_jv_j^\top$, is the **best rank-$p$ approximation of $A$ in Frobenius norm** (the Eckart–Young theorem) — the basis for image compression by a low-rank approximation, and for the SVD-based methods that dominated approaches like the Netflix Prize. Applying the SVD to a vector, $UDV^\top x$, has a clean transformation reading: $V^\top x$ expresses $x$ in the basis given by $V$'s columns, multiplying by $D$ stretches those coordinates, and multiplying by $U$ reassembles the result in the basis given by $U$'s columns — the SVD carries $x$ from the column space of $V$ to the column space of $U$. **Computing it.** The Golub–Reinsch algorithm mirrors the QR algorithm for eigendecompositions: Householder transformations on both sides reduce $A$ to upper bidiagonal form, and repeated Givens transformations then converge this to the diagonal $D$, with $U$ and $V$ accumulated as products of the transformations used along the way (a final adjustment fixes signs and sorts the singular values). For a **tall-skinny** matrix ($n \gg p$), it is cheaper to first compute $X = QR$ and then take the SVD of the small $p\times p$ matrix $R = U^*DV^\top$, giving $X = QU^*DV^\top$. ## Exploiting structure: fast libraries, sparsity, low-rank updates ### BLAS and LAPACK Matrix operations in R and Python drop into compiled C or Fortran with little intervening interpreted code, via two core libraries: **BLAS** (Basic Linear Algebra Subroutines: vector operations, matrix-vector operations, dense matrix-matrix operations) and **LAPACK**, built on top of BLAS, which implements the standard algorithms — eigendecomposition, linear solves, factorizations. Which *implementation* of BLAS numpy or R is linked against (OpenBLAS, Intel MKL, AMD's ACML, Apple's vecLib — which on Apple-silicon Macs uses the AMX co-processor) matters a great deal for speed, since these can be threaded to use multiple cores. (Conda-installed numpy is typically linked to MKL or OpenBLAS; pip-installed numpy typically to OpenBLAS.) Packages such as JAX and PyTorch provide alternative implementations that can also target a GPU automatically. ### Sparse and banded matrices Symmetric, triangular, diagonal, banded and block-diagonal matrices all admit compact storage and faster operations than treating them as dense. A **banded** matrix with lower bandwidth $p$ and upper bandwidth $q$ ($A_{ij}=0$ for $i>j+p$ or $j>i+q$) has an LU factorization costing $O(npq)$ rather than $O(n^3)$, and the resulting triangular solves cost $O(np+nq)$ — a large saving for small $p,q$. Banded covariance structures arise naturally, e.g. from moving-average time series models, whose covariance vanishes beyond a fixed lag. A standard sparse layout is **CSR (compressed sparse row)**: store the non-zero entries row by row in an array `data`, an array `indptr` giving the position of each row's first entry, and an array `indices` giving each entry's column: ```python import scipy.sparse as sparse mat = np.array([[0,0,1,0,10],[0,0,0,100,0],[0,0,0,0,0],[1000,0,0,0,0]]) mat = sparse.csr_array(mat) mat.data, mat.indices, mat.indptr ``` A sparse matrix-vector multiply then costs only $O(k)$ multiplies and additions, where $k$ is the number of non-zero entries — versus $O(n^2)$ for the dense version. If a sparse matrix's *pattern* of non-zeros is fixed but its entries change (e.g. across iterations of a fitting algorithm), the reordering that best preserves sparsity in a Cholesky factor can be precomputed once and reused. ### Low-rank updates (optional) A **rank-one update** of $A$ is $A - uv^\top$; more generally a **low-rank update** is $\tilde A = A - UV^\top$ with $U,V$ of size $n\times m$, $m \ll n$. The **Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury** identity gives the inverse of the update from the inverse of $A$: $$\tilde A^{-1} = A^{-1} + A^{-1}U\big(I_m - V^\top A^{-1}U\big)^{-1}V^\top A^{-1}.$$ If $x_0 = A^{-1}b$ is already known, the solution to $\tilde A x = b$ follows without re-solving the whole system from scratch, since the only new work is with the $m\times m$ matrix $I_m - V^\top A^{-1}U$. A related form, $\tilde A = A + UCV^\top$, gives $\tilde A^{-1} = A^{-1} - A^{-1}U(C^{-1} +V^\top A^{-1}U)^{-1}V^\top A^{-1}$ — useful in Bayesian settings where a precision matrix $A^{-1}$ is available directly (precisions often add when combining independent sources of information) but the covariance $A$ is not. In short, the identity lets a smart way of solving one system carry over to a low-rank perturbation of it. ## Iterative solutions of linear systems (optional) Both methods below trade the guarantee of an exact answer for the option to stop early, which is the point of using them at all on large problems. ### Gauss–Seidel Starting from $x^{(0)}$, update one coordinate of $x$ at a time by solving the corresponding equation with everything else held fixed: $x_1^{(1)} = \tfrac{1}{a_{11}}\big(b_1 - \sum_{j\geq 2}a_{1j}x_j^{(0)}\big)$, then the same for each remaining coordinate to get $x^{(1)}$, and iterate until $\|x^{(k)}-x^{(k-1)}\|$ (or the residual's change) is small enough. Writing $A = L+D+U$ ($L,U$ strictly lower/upper triangular), one update step solves $(L+D)x^{(k+1)} = b - Ux^{(k)}$, an $O(n^2)$ triangular solve, so each full sweep is $O(n^2)$ rather than the $O(n^3)$ of an exact factorization — a saving whenever convergence happens well before $n$ iterations. The rate of convergence is governed by the spectral radius of $(L+D)^{-1}U$. Geometrically, Gauss–Seidel moves only in axis-aligned directions, which can make it slow. ### Conjugate gradient For positive definite $A$, solving $Ax=b$ is equivalent to minimizing $f(x) = \tfrac12 x^\top A x - x^\top b$ (its gradient is $Ax - b$, zero exactly at the solution). Rather than following the gradient at each step (*steepest descent*, which can converge slowly), **conjugate gradient** chooses a sequence of directions $d_k$ that are mutually **$A$-conjugate**, $d_i^\top A d_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$, moving $x_{(k)} = x_{(k-1)} + \alpha_k d_k$. Starting from $x_{(0)}$ with residual $r_{(0)} = b - Ax_{(0)}$ and direction $d_0 = r_{(0)}$, each iteration computes $$\alpha_k = \frac{r_{(k)}^\top r_{(k)}}{d_k^\top A d_k}, \qquad x_{(k+1)} = x_{(k)} + \alpha_k d_k, \qquad r_{(k+1)} = r_{(k)} - \alpha_k A d_k, \qquad d_{k+1} = r_{(k+1)} + \frac{r_{(k+1)}^\top r_{(k+1)}}{r_{(k)}^\top r_{(k)}}\,d_k,$$ stopping once $\|r^{(k+1)}\|$ is small. (The last step is a Gram–Schmidt-style update: it would need to remove components along every previous direction, but it turns out $r_{(k+1)}$ is already $A$-orthogonal to all but the most recent one.) In exact arithmetic CG reaches the exact answer in $n$ steps, but its real use is as an *approximation* stopped well before that, for large sparse positive-definite systems; convergence is faster when the condition number is smaller (eigenvalues not too spread out). Geometrically it moves in axis-aligned directions of a space that has been stretched by $A$. ### Updating a solution Having solved $Ax=b$, solving $Ax=c$ for a new right-hand side reuses the existing factorization at $O(n^2)$ rather than repeating the full $O(n^3)$ factorization. If $c = b + \delta b$ is close to $b$, an iterative method (Gauss–Seidel or CG) started from the old solution $x^{(0)}$ typically converges very quickly. ## Sources All of this chapter comes from Unit 10, "Numerical linear algebra," of UC Berkeley's STAT 243 (Statistical Computing), taught by Chris Paciorek.
